frames.narration: 1,000 requests arrive every second and each stays in the service for 50 ms. Little's law: L = lambda x W = 1,000 per second x 0.05 s = 50 requests in flight on average. No assumption about distributions is needed.
50 workers would be busy 100% of the time, with no room for randomness. Aim for 70% busy: 50 / 0.7 = 72 workers. Utilisation is now 50 / 72 = 69%.
Think of the pool as one fast server to see the curve. At 50% busy, time in system is 50 ms / (1 - 0.5) = 100 ms: queueing doubles the latency.
At 90% busy the same formula gives 50 / 0.1 = 500 ms. The load rose only 80% (0.5 to 0.9) but latency rose 5x. Randomness means bursts find all workers busy and the queue never fully drains.
At 99% busy: 50 / 0.01 = 5,000 ms, 100x the service time. Going from 90% to 99% (10% more traffic) made latency 10x worse. Clients with a 1 second timeout now give up on most requests.

Timed-out clients retry. If 10% of requests are retried, offered load rises by 10%: 90% busy becomes 99% busy, which causes more timeouts and more retries. The queue grows faster than the pool can drain it.

Fixes act on arrivals and the queue: a bounded queue that rejects early, retries with backoff and a budget, and capacity added before the knee. Rejected requests fail in milliseconds instead of waiting 5 seconds.

Shared queue vs separate queues matters too. 72 workers on one shared queue wait about 0.005 ms on average at 69% busy. 72 private queues behave like 72 separate single servers: a wait of about 114 ms at the same load.
